body_md: HTTP is stateless request-response over TCP. Client sends method, path, headers; server returns status plus body. HTTPS adds TLS. Keep requests idempotent where possible and cache GETs.
code:
GET /feed?page=2 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.ferrisfeed.dev

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
hook: HTTP is stateless: the protocol every design builds on.

quiz.explain: Each request carries its full context, so a load balancer can send it to any identical instance; add servers without sharing session state.
options: Sticky sessions keep each user on one server
Any instance can serve any request
It keeps one TCP socket per client open
It limits HTTP to cacheable static files
quiz.q: Why does HTTP's statelessness help you scale?

takeaway: Design stateless handlers that scale horizontally.
trap: Storing session in server memory breaks scaling.

body_md: REST uses resources plus verbs: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH merges, DELETE removes. Return 201 with Location on create, 404 for missing, 409 for conflicts. Version via /v1.
hook: REST done right: resources, verbs, status codes.

quiz.explain: REST names entities as nouns (/users/42) and lets GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE express the action, with real status codes.
options: HTTP verbs acting on noun resource URLs
Verb URLs like /getUser called with GET
One POST endpoint with an action field
Custom JSON status flags, always 200 OK
quiz.q: How does idiomatic REST model operations?

takeaway: Name resources as nouns, act with verbs.

body_md: gRPC uses Protobuf over HTTP/2 with streaming. Define service in .proto, generate stubs, get typed clients in any language. Great for internal microservices needing speed and contracts.
hook: gRPC: typed Protobuf contracts at binary speed.
output:
protoc emits typed Feed client + server stubs (any language)
ListPosts: unary RPC; StreamPosts: server-streaming RPC

quiz.explain: gRPC generates typed stubs from .proto files and sends compact binary Protobuf over multiplexed HTTP/2, with streaming built in.
options: It sends JSON over HTTP/1.1 for easy debugging
It wraps calls in XML envelopes like SOAP
Typed Protobuf contracts over HTTP/2 streams
It sends untyped strings over raw sockets
quiz.q: Why is gRPC popular for internal microservices?

takeaway: Use gRPC for fast internal service calls.
trap: Exposing gRPC directly to browsers without gateway.

body_md: GraphQL lets clients request exactly fields they need in one query. Server defines schema and resolvers. Solves over-fetching but needs query cost limits and persisted queries to avoid abuse.
hook: GraphQL: one query, exactly the fields you want.
output:
{"data": {"post": {"title": "...", "author": {"name": "..."}}}}
// exactly the requested fields, one round trip

quiz.explain: Clients describe the exact shape they need in one query, avoiding over-fetching and chained round trips. The schema still constrains queries.
options: Receive full table rows on every request
Send raw SQL straight to the backing database
Request exactly the fields it needs in one go
Skip the schema and send any query shape
quiz.q: What does GraphQL let a client do?

takeaway: Choose GraphQL for flexible client-driven reads.

body_md: WebSocket upgrades HTTP to full-duplex frames. Handshake once, then both sides push. Ideal for chat and presence. Add heartbeats, resume tokens, and horizontal sticky or pub/sub fan-out.
hook: WebSockets: one handshake, endless push both ways.
output:
101 Switching Protocols -> socket open
send({"t":"hi"}); each inbound frame -> render(data)

quiz.explain: After one HTTP upgrade handshake the socket stays open and either side can push frames instantly, without per-message headers or polling.
options: Each message gets its own fresh HTTP request
Both sides push over one open connection
They guarantee delivery even when offline
They work without any server-side state
quiz.q: Why use WebSockets over HTTP polling for chat?

takeaway: Use WebSockets for low-latency bidirectional push.
trap: No heartbeat so dead peers linger.

body_md: SQL gives ACID, joins, and schema; NoSQL gives flexible scale-out for keys, docs, or wide rows. Choose Postgres for relations and transactions, Dynamo-style KV for massive simple lookups.
hook: SQL vs NoSQL: pick by query pattern, not by hype.
output:
CREATE TABLE
// posts(id, author_id, body) ready; writes ACID, PK-indexed

quiz.explain: Model queries first: relational joins and multi-row transactions favor SQL; huge volumes of simple key or document lookups favor NoSQL.
options: Your query patterns: joins vs key lookups
NoSQL is the modern default for every app
SQL databases can never scale horizontally
Both offer identical consistency and scaling
quiz.q: What should guide the choice of SQL vs NoSQL?

takeaway: Model queries first, then pick the store.
trap: Storing graphs in relational joins at depth 5.

body_md: Redis is in-memory with strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, and streams. Use for cache, counters, leaderboards, and rate limits. Persist with AOF+RDB and cluster when memory exceeds one node.
code:
SET post:42 1 EX 3600
ZADD leaderboard 950 user:7
GET post:42
hook: Redis is a data-structure server living in RAM.

quiz.explain: Redis keeps hashes, sets, sorted sets, and counters in RAM, so caching, rate limits, and leaderboards run in well under a millisecond.
options: It is cheap cold storage for archived documents
It replaces SQL for all transactional writes
In-memory data structures with sub-ms access
It guarantees durability stronger than Postgres
quiz.q: Why do architectures add Redis next to the main DB?

takeaway: Put hot, ephemeral, or ranked data in Redis.
trap: Treating cache as source of truth without TTL.

body_md: Load balancers spread traffic: L4 by connection, L7 by URL/header. Algorithms include round-robin, least-conn, and consistent hash. Health-check backends and drain before deploy.
hook: Load balancers make sure no single server feels famous.

quiz.explain: Health checks remove failing nodes from rotation, and algorithms like least-connections or round-robin spread requests across the rest.
options: All traffic goes to one primary until it fails
Spreads requests across healthy servers only
Relies on DNS alone, without checking servers
Caches writes locally so backends do less
quiz.q: How does a load balancer protect backends in a surge?

takeaway: Balance plus health-check for resilient tiers.

body_md: CDNs cache static assets at edge PoPs near users. Origin sets Cache-Control, CDN serves hits in ms. Use versioned URLs for immutable assets and purge on deploy for HTML.
code:
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
# app.abc123.js cached at edge
hook: CDNs serve your static assets in milliseconds, worldwide.
output:
Edge HIT: app.abc123.js served from PoP in ms
immutable -> no revalidation for 1 year

quiz.explain: Edge servers in many regions hold cached copies, so users fetch from nearby instead of a distant origin, cutting round-trip time.
options: It compresses each asset once at the origin
It routes users to the least busy origin
It serves video only, not scripts or images
It caches assets at edge PoPs near users
quiz.q: How does a CDN cut latency for static assets?

takeaway: Cache immutable assets at the edge.
trap: Caching personalized HTML at edge leaks data.

body_md: Latency vs throughput: latency is time per request, throughput is requests per second. CDN and caching cut latency; horizontal scale and batching raise throughput. Measure p95, not averages.
hook: Latency vs throughput: fast once vs fast often.

quiz.explain: A fast average can hide 5% of requests stalling for seconds from queueing or GC pauses; p95 and p99 expose that tail.
options: Averages hide slow tails that users feel
Tail and average latency are always equal
Averages already reflect the worst case
Throughput rises whenever averages rise
quiz.q: Why track p95/p99 latency, not just the average?

takeaway: Track p95 latency and max throughput separately.

body_md: Polling vs push: short-poll wastes requests, long-poll holds open, SSE streams one-way, WebSocket is bidirectional. Choose SSE for feeds, WebSocket for chat.
code:
const es = new EventSource("/events");
es.onmessage = (e) => console.log(e.data);
hook: Polling vs push: stop polling, start streaming.
output:
HTTP 200 text/event-stream held open
// each server event -> console.log(data); one-way push, no polling

quiz.explain: SSE streams server-to-client over plain HTTP and suits feeds and tickers; pick WebSockets when the client must stream upstream too.
options: SSE is deprecated, so always use WebSockets
Short polling is lighter than either one
Whether the client must also push data
WebSockets cannot pass through proxies
quiz.q: SSE or WebSockets: what decides the choice?

trap: Polling a feed every second from a million clients.

body_md: API pagination: cursor-based with `after_id` scales, offset breaks on inserts. Return `next_cursor` and limit. Order by indexed (created_at, id) for stable pages.
code:
SELECT * FROM posts
WHERE id < $1 ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20;
hook: Cursor pagination: pages that survive new inserts.

quiz.explain: OFFSET counts rows, so inserts at the top shift items across pages. WHERE id < :last_seen anchors to a row, and an index keeps it fast.
options: OFFSET is immune to rows shifting on insert
New posts can't shift items between pages
Cursors remove the need for any index
OFFSET results can't be cached by the CDN
quiz.q: Why is cursor pagination better than OFFSET for feeds?

takeaway: Paginate by cursor on indexed columns.

body_md: Caching levels: browser, CDN, LB, app, Redis, DB. Cache-aside reads Redis then DB on miss. Set TTLs, version keys, and invalidate on write. Stampede-protect with singleflight.
code:
val = redis.get(k)
if !val:
  val = db.load(k)
  redis.setex(k, 300, val)
hook: Cache layers: each one can save your database.
output:
1st call: miss -> db.load(k), SETEX k 300
later calls: Redis hit in ms, zero DB load

quiz.explain: The app owns the logic: check cache, load from the DB on a miss, write it back with a TTL. A cache that loads itself is read-through.
options: The app reads the DB, then fills the cache
The database pushes the row into the cache
The cache fetches from the DB on its own
The miss errors and the client retries
quiz.q: In cache-aside, what happens on a cache miss?

takeaway: Read cache first, fill on miss with TTL.
trap: No TTL causing permanently stale reads.

body_md: Status codes matter: 2xx success, 301/304 redirect/cache, 400 bad input, 401 unauth, 403 forbidden, 404 missing, 429 slow down, 5xx server fault. Retry only 429/5xx with backoff.
hook: HTTP status codes are contracts, so honor them.
output:
Client waits 2s (Retry-After), retries with backoff
// retry 429/5xx only; 400-class means fix the request

quiz.explain: 429 means you hit a rate limit. Waiting for Retry-After and backing off with jitter avoids hammering a server that is already overloaded.
options: Retry right away, since 429s clear quickly
Treat it like a 404 and stop for good
Switch API keys to get a fresh quota
Wait as told, then retry with backoff
quiz.q: How should a client handle 429 with Retry-After?

takeaway: Signal precisely so retries behave correctly.
trap: Returning 200 with error JSON breaks tooling.

body_md: Monolith vs microservices: start modular monolith, extract when teams or scale demand. Microservices add deploy freedom but need discovery, tracing, and versioned contracts.
hook: Monolith first, microservices when it starts to hurt.

quiz.explain: A modular monolith is fast to change. Extract services when team boundaries or distinct scaling needs justify the network cost.
options: Microservices from day one, to scale early
A modular monolith; split when it hurts
A monolith forever; services never pay off
One service per database table from day one
quiz.q: Monolith or microservices for a new product?

takeaway: Split by team or scaling pressure, not hype.
trap: Distributed monolith with all the costs, none of the gains.
